name: Books, Mentor Texts, and Current Events
title: Books, Mentor Texts, and Current Events
answer: AI can help students find books they want to read, give teachers model paragraphs for a writing skill, and draft discussion questions for a book club or a news story. The serious catch is that chatbots sometimes invent books and resources that do not exist, so every title must be checked against the school library catalog and every model example must be checked by the teacher before students use it.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea covers three ways AI supports reading and writing work: matching students to books, producing mentor texts, and helping with current events and book discussions. A student describes what they liked about a recent book, and a tool suggests titles at a similar level and topic. Mentor texts are short examples of the kind of writing students are learning to do, such as a strong opening or a clear counterargument. For current events, services like Newsela offer news articles at several reading levels so a whole class can discuss the same story. The problem these uses solve is preparation time and student engagement, since more students stay in the same conversation and teachers spend less time assembling materials.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not separate these uses by grade band, though the chapter covers kindergarten through twelfth grade, so the same three moves apply across the years. For book choice, a student describes what they liked about a recent book and a tool suggests titles at a similar level and topic, and the suggestion is checked against the school library catalog before the student goes looking. For writing, a teacher asks an AI tool for several model paragraphs showing a particular skill, such as a strong opening or a clear counterargument, written at different levels, and students study what makes each example work before trying the technique in their own writing. For discussion, a teacher can use AI to draft questions for a book club and then adapt them to the group, or use leveled news articles so a whole class can talk about the same story. In every case the teacher prepares the material first and the students work with it afterward.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives one research reference and no formal evidence label. It reports that chatbots sometimes invent books that do not exist, the same kind of error researchers found when a chatbot listed a teaching resource that could not be found (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). Beyond that finding, the text offers no study, figure or measured result for the book matching, mentor text or discussion question uses, so those rest on practice rather than research. The practical response the text draws from the finding is that every suggestion should be checked against the school library catalog before a student goes looking for it.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk named in the text is invention: a chatbot may suggest a book that does not exist, so no title reaches a student unchecked. The check belongs to a person, and the text places it at the school library catalog before the student goes looking. For mentor texts, the teacher checks the examples first and uses them as models, not as templates to copy, which keeps the writing work with the student. For discussion questions, the teacher drafts with AI and then adapts the questions to the group, so the judgment about what fits a particular class stays with the teacher. These are practice decisions, not legal advice, and the text leaves them with the teacher and the school.
